newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Sharif says Pakistan must improve tarnished image.
newsitem.headline: Sharif says Pakistan must improve tarnished image.

text.p: Former Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, whose Pakistan Muslim League is front-runner in next month's polls, said on Monday that Pakistan had become a laughing stock and must clean up its tarnished reputation.

He said the PML would do well in the February 3 elections, called by President Farooq Leghari after he dissolved the National Assembly (lower house) and sacked Benazir Bhutto's government on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.

"Pakistan needs now to project a new image in the world," Sharif told Reuters in an interview. "We have become a laughing stock where every time the president and prime minister are fighting one another. This must now come to an end."
Bhutto's was the fourth elected government in eight years to be dismissed by a president under the controversial Eighth Amendment to the constitution.

Sharif, whose own government was toppled under the amendment in 1993, took a cautious line when asked if a PML government would try to scrap the legislation and refused to say if he believed that the president should enjoy such powers.
"That is an issue that needs to be debated in parliament," he said. "The new parliament will certainly debate that issue."

Sharif, 52, was also cagey about whether a PML government would retain a Council for Defence and National Security formed this month by Leghari and his caretaker cabinet, giving the military its first formal advisory role in government affairs.
"This is a subject we will discuss later," he said. "I think the first emphasis is to fight the elections. Once we are in parliament, the parliament will take that decision."

He said the military, which has ruled Pakistan for 24 years in its 50-year history, should avoid politics, but endorsed the previous system of informal meetings between the so-called troika of president, prime minister and chief of army staff.
"There is no harm in that, and these informal consultations must carry on," Sharif declared.
He said that PML administrations in the centre and provinces would tackle law and order problems, put the economy right and eliminate corruption from society, politics and government.
He vowed to pursue an anti-corruption drive begun by the caretakers and to ensure that the Ehtesab (Accountability) Commission worked independently free of government influence.

"The need of the hour is to have a strong, stable government and that can only happen with a comfortable majority in parliament," he said. "We have so much to do. The revival of the economy will be a very uphill task."
Sharif, whose family has an industrial empire based in the Punjab provincial capital Lahore, said he would uphold any agreements made with the International Monetary Fund.
"We consider them the commitments of Pakistan, not of any one government or any one party," he added.

Sharif said the PML's agenda dovetailed with IMF views on how Pakistan can climb out of its economic crisis. The PML would aim to get rid of government fat, cut non-development spending, boost revenues and restore investor confidence.
The PML leader said that if his party came to power it would seek a working relationship with the opposition, cooperating on national issues.
He also foresaw cooperation with Leghari, a former close Bhutto ally, despite past PML accusations that the president was involved in a scandal surrounding the collapsed Mehran Bank.
"We'd like to make a new beginning," Sharif said. "We'll try to work together...and we would like to live as friends, as good partners. I don't think it will be very difficult."
